notes: This is the one case where a company fought back, and the decision is the most useful document in the batch because a judge construes the repayment clause. Three holdings. First, on the clause itself: "the Court finds that the Grant Agreement clearly and unambiguously provided that Plaintiff may recover the entire amount of the grant upon a breach," following State Dep't of Dev. v. Matrix Centennial, LLC, 2014-Ohio-3251. Second, on timing: the WARN notice was "a clear, overt, and unequivocal repudiation and anticipatory breach," so JobsOhio could sue immediately without waiting for the Metric Evaluation Date. Third, and the one that matters most for the post, on fairness. MITEC argued that its parent had filed for insolvency in Germany in November 2018, that it lost General Motors as its main customer when GM moved engine-component work to Mexico, that it had asked JobsOhio to waive repayment, and that JobsOhio's "strictly and hastily enforcing the collection remedy ... without granting Defendant any relief under the circumstances presented and in the midst of a global pandemic, is unreasonable and a breach of the implied duty to act in good faith and deal fairly." The court rejected it: "Ohio law holds that an implied duty of good faith cannot be used to prevent a party from exercising remedies expressly afforded it under a contract," citing Adams v. LCI Int'l Telecom Corp. So the discretion in "all or a portion" belongs to JobsOhio alone, and a company cannot argue in court that taking all of it was unfair. I read the complaint, the decision and the final judgment. I did not read the 37-page summary judgment motion or the company's 20-page opposition in full.

notes: The judgment is $8,000 larger than the complaint asked for, and the reason is traceable on the record. JobsOhio's memorandum in support of default judgment opens: "JobsOhio filed this Complaint on June 11, 2026, seeking recovery of $25,000.00 in grant funds pursuant to Defendant's breach of a Grant Agreement entered into with JobsOhio." The complaint says $17,000.00 five times, including in its prayer, and never says $25,000.00 except as the ceiling of the award. $25,000.00 is the amount the agreement authorized, not the amount JobsOhio pleaded it paid out. The court signed the entry at $25,000.00 against a company that was never personally served, was served through the Secretary of State because its statutory agent's address was bad, and never appeared. I verified this by reading the complaint, the default motion and the judgment entry; I did not find any amended complaint or any filing correcting the figure. I am reporting what the documents say and not asserting an explanation. The underlying facts are also the smallest in the batch: a Port Clinton company that promised six jobs, and the pleaded breach is a missing 2025 Annual Report, with the metric failure alleged only on information and belief.
